subject: Business
title: Free Trade Agreements and Tariffs
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Free Trade Agreements and Tariffs.

hook.text: A 25% tariff on Chinese goods added $800 to the cost of a shipping container overnight. Supply chains scrambled.

buildup.text: Tariffs are taxes on imports. Free trade agreements remove or reduce them between partner countries.

discovery.text: NAFTA (now USMCA) eliminated most tariffs between the US, Canada, and Mexico, creating a massive free trade zone.

twist.text: Trade wars use tariffs as weapons. The US-China trade war disrupted supply chains that took decades to build.

climax.text: Companies now 'friend-shore' — shifting production to allied countries to reduce tariff and political risk.

punchline.text: Tariffs change the math. Supply chains follow the math.

quiz.question: What is 'friend-shoring'?
options: Shifting production to allied countries to reduce geopolitical risk
Building warehouses near the coast for faster shipping
Sharing supply chain data with competitors

details.summary: Free trade agreements reduce or eliminate tariffs between member countries while tariffs impose taxes on imported goods. These trade policies directly impact supply chain costs, sourcing decisions, and the geographic configuration of manufacturing and distribution networks.
details.whyItMatters: Trade policy changes can instantly alter the cost calculus of global supply chains. Companies must understand tariff structures and trade agreements to optimize sourcing locations and avoid unexpected cost increases from geopolitical shifts.
takeaways: FTAs reduce tariffs between member nations to encourage bilateral trade
Rules of origin determine whether goods qualify for preferential tariff rates
Trade policy shifts can force rapid supply chain reconfiguration

faq.question: How do rules of origin affect supply chain decisions?
faq.answer: To qualify for reduced tariffs under an FTA, products must meet rules of origin proving sufficient local content or transformation. This influences where companies source components and locate manufacturing to ensure products qualify for preferential treatment.

faq.question: How should companies prepare for sudden tariff changes?
faq.answer: Maintain a diversified supplier base across trade zones, model tariff scenarios in total landed cost calculations, build relationships with customs brokers, classify products accurately for correct duty rates, and monitor geopolitical developments proactively.
